source.citation: Nyamnjoh and Fuh, Njangi sociality (IMTFI blog), Universepg paper on ROSCAs in the Western Region, Development and Cooperation on tontines, and a paper on informal financial associations. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: A rotating savings and credit association (ROSCA) in which members pool money at agreed, regular intervals and each member receives the pot in turn.
attributes.names: Njangi among Anglophone Cameroonians and tontine among Francophones. Other names for the same idea elsewhere include esusu in Nigeria.
attributes.language: Members say they play njangi, and the member who receives the money is said to chop njangi, although they are expected to invest it wisely and not waste it.
attributes.saying: A well-known saying is life na njangi, meaning life is give and take.
attributes.rules: Each njangi has its own rules, and trust and shared values among members are important.
attributes.purpose: Savings, loans and social support, including paying school fees, in places where banks are scarce or distant.
attributes.loan_effect: A member who receives early gets what is in effect an interest-free loan, and one who receives late uses it as savings.
attributes.bamileke: The Bamileke of the Western Region use these associations extensively to finance small businesses, using names such as tontine, njangi and Ntshwa.
attributes.technology: A study of mobile money found that electronic money was making njangi transactions more secure.
attributes.origin_of_word_tontine: The French word is said to come from the Italian banker Lorenzo Tonti, who suggested a mutual insurance scheme in the 17th century.

source.citation: Cambridge University Press, Africa journal, Urbanites and urban villagers (2011). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

content.name: Hometown associations of the Bamileke in Yaoundé

attributes.description: Associations of people from the same home area living in a city, in this study Bamileke women from Ndé Division living in Yaoundé.
attributes.kinds: Elite associations, whose members are urbanites with diverse social networks and a universal language about bringing development to the hometown, and non-elite neighbourhood associations, which resemble dense urban villages that try to bring home to the city.
attributes.meaning: They help members feel they belong, and emotions of memory, marginalisation and recognition shape what home means.
attributes.source_type: An academic study published in the journal Africa.
